mainText:
If you only remember one thing: the Jensen Huang scandal has turned chip export controls into a live political fight in Washington.

Number one. Nvidia and Jensen Huang. From your Politico Decoded. Huang is under pressure over an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who may have routed sensitive technology to China. Nvidia's board has opened an outside investigation, and a shareholder lawsuit has already been filed. Analysts at Bernstein say Huang pulls most of the company's strings, and nobody is obviously waiting to replace him. President Trump says Huang is in good shape. But Republicans including Brett Guthrie and Jim Banks want investigations. China hawks in both parties are using this to push export control legislation during the lame duck session. Your Rundown adds that Nvidia's top lawyer reportedly emailed investigators in August twenty twenty five, about whether Singapore's Megaspeed smuggled chips to China, before that case was halted and handed to the Justice Department. Why it matters: Nvidia's fate and U S chip policy are now tied together.

Number two. A I models and chips. From your Rundown. Anthropic released Claude Fable five point two and Mythos five point two. Fable took the number one spot on the Artificial Analysis leaderboard, ahead of Google's unreleased Gemini four Carbon. It's twenty percent cheaper and up to thirty percent faster than version five point one. Anthropic says it's pacing, not pausing. Mythos stays limited to vetted security and life science groups. Meta released Muse Ember, a small, cheap model for agents, which matches Claude Haiku five point five at about one third of the cost per task. And Google announced two new T P U chips, aimed at Nvidia, one built to keep data encrypted even while the model works on it. Also, the Wall Street Journal reports Anthropic is preparing to go ahead with its I P O, possibly as soon as next Thursday. And Fireworks, an open source A I hosting startup, confirmed a hack that exposed customer billing details and parts of some models. Why it matters: the frontier keeps moving, and the competition is now about cost and custom chips.

Number three. A I safety and policy. New York Governor Kathy Hochul is launching a first in the nation center to independently test A I systems. It's funded by thirty million dollars from Tom Secunda, plus twenty five million from the state and SUNY, and it opens ahead of New York's RAISE Act, which takes effect January first. Meanwhile in Paris, Emmanuel Macron collected signatures from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google DeepMind and Hugging Face on a Paris Call for A I Safety. It calls for independent evaluators, shared standards for reporting major incidents, and clearer responsibilities. And from your E U A I Act newsletter: the A I Office has proposed qualification and independence rules for outside evaluators of the biggest models, and has sent information requests to more than thirty providers. Fines are possible. Former Biden A I adviser Ben Buchanan is urging Democrats to move fast on A I rules, and floated banning recursive self improvement, where models build better models without human oversight. Why it matters: everyone is converging on independent testing, but nobody agrees who does it.

Number four. Tech geopolitics and good news. From your Recode China A I newsletter: Ulanqab, a remote Chinese city that used to be mostly farming, is turning into an A I computing hub and a magnet for young workers. Also in your Reads, your A I Collective newsletter argues the agentic internet needs a way to prove who agents are, and what they're allowed to do. For the media side, Adobe signed a multi year deal with Disney to build custom models trained on Disney's characters. Why it matters: A I infrastructure is spreading to unexpected places, and trust and identity are the missing layer.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker is looking at what the Huang affair means for Nvidia, and why Russia and Ukraine haven't made a deal. GalleriesNow has its week in art, and the Washington Post's The Seven covers hacked I C E data.

The thread today: power, testing and trust. Who controls the chips, who tests the models, and who can prove what an agent is. Have a good day, Sin.
